segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You have already been here, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, I’ve spoken already.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They have already told you the reason why they are doing this?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, they told me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She wrote some of these I think, ain’t it? [Questions]

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We helped out with that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. What is your name in English and Cherokee?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: In English, Cora Flute is my name, and in Cherokee, Dayeni.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Dayeni.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes. My grandmother had the same name. In English her name was Cora, and in Cherokee Dayeni was her name.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is where you got it from, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, Dad named me that, gave me that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you were just a child, just a girl, it asks, what did you have to play with, things that you made yourself?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Sometimes we made things. As for me I didn’t hardly play with dolls. I always liked playing guitar. That was the only thing I was given, that they bought. At Christmas they gave me that. It was just play, it was not real.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It wasn’t real?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: No. But as for things to play with—we made different things. Like, we made things from clay like plates. We would act like we were cooking. Even more when it rained. Then it went down. That’s when the clay was soft. We would make things. And leaves, slender leaves. That we would get them off the plant, and pretend they were money. I would have leaves this thick [gestures].

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were really rich.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I was rich, I was wealthy. We made different things. I was telling the students. There was a little pond that was made there, where we lived, or where we still live. But there was an old house near there, and that’s where it was, there. We would get a board, and cut it—a foot, or half a foot. We would make boats from that. As for me, I would put nails on the end of it, two or three inches apart. And those rubbers they put around their hair [rubber bands, hairbands].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They put around with, yeah.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yeah, I used one like that. Then I would slice a piece of wood, about an inch wide. I would stick it between there [the rubber bands] and turn it. And, when I would let it go, it would go by itself—like a boat.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man!

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We did different things. We didn’t have lots of things to play with.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you not see them before, already? Those kind you were making. [play boats]

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Umm...

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And you learned to make them?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I may have [seen that style of toy boat] when we were given a TV. When we got one. How old was I? I don’t know. I don’t remember. I was in second-ten, or third grade. Then we bought one [TV]. I probably seen it there. I don’t remember good. Also, those boys had little play cars. But all of us were the older, us girls. One was named Archie—he was the oldest of the boys. He was little, back then. They would give him lots of things to play with, because he was the only boy.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And you girls had to make it yourself?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes. It was then that we probably seen [TV]. Because we would act like policeman, sometime. We didn’t have guns or anything. Sometimes sticks, we used sticks, and also our hands.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did y’all climb trees, too?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, we climbed them. And, if they had big limbs, we would lay old boards across there and get up there. We had a place to climb up, would stick nails [in].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did y’all build ‘kind of a house?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was her making noise, when I went outside.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: In the summer we were always outside. We hardly were inside the house. When we were growing up, they gave us each a bicycle. We would run around everywhere, riding them on the road. No matter how hot it was, we would still be running around.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Y’all must have been enjoying the wind blowing on you, when it goes fast.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That’s it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What, those mud pies, did you all not make them, too?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, with the clay. We used to really make them in the mud. And we would slice them up when they dried a little bit. We would give them to each other.
[laughter]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You were talking about bicycles. When Rudy first got one, it was big. We really rode it, when he would bring it to the house. The last time I rode it... Do you know where it goes up the hill, by Dad’s? We would turn around there. When I turned around there, someone came out—I fell off. [laughter] It scared me. It was good back then, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: It was good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I wonder why, when you think back, some will say, “we were poor back then...” But, if you think about it, we had a good past.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That’s true. Dad used to say that all the time. He would say, “I grew up poor--We grew up poor, but it was good. We loved each other.” He said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: As far as money, we were poor. But as for living—it was good.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Our lives were good. We would be laughing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And also --

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We would meet. It was a good feeling.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: -- and, when we would go to town, we didn’t lock the doors. Or, if we went somewhere, we didn’t lock the doors.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We didn’t hardly go to town. Every month, I think, they would take us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And, there would be buckets of water hanging on the porch. And one dipper. When someone went by, someone would get [them] a drink of water. It was like that, back then.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We had a well. It was cold, it was good. I get thirsty for that, sometimes. But nowadays they said, it’s bad. “It is not good to drink,” they said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: “There are too many different waters going through. And that is what made it bad. It is not good. It will make your body sick,” they told us. We would draw out a bucket full every morning and every evening. There would be cold water all the time. And we would use one dipper, and drink.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And even if someone came --

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: -- they used the same one.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Grandpa and Grandma had it like that. And, all the people that went by used it. Not now.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: People will not do that now. They will get scared.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Back then, we didn’t care did we?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Huh uh. Huh uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That is why we were healthier. Thinking about things sometimes makes us sick.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That is true.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes... Who was it that said that to me? That what I was thinking about was making me sick, they told me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s probably true.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That will make you sick.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “One of these days, when you don’t want something...” What was it they said to me? “One of these days, what you are saying is going to come true,” [they said.] “Like, for instance, if there is something you are not liking. If you are saying, “Eew,” and not liking it. That is going to be the only thing you have to eat,” they told me.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That is what they would tell us. “Like, things, don’t be disgusted with things—someone eats it.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: “Do not waste food.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now we waste a lot, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: At church when we eat, when the children are there, they will put a lot and just eat very little.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Just one thing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They will carry it by.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They will throw it away.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is what I don’t like, is to waste food.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A long time ago. I went toward the north, where others live. We had a Bible school event. It was in South Dakota, Lower Brule Reservation [Lower Brule Sioux Tribe]. The [Sioux] children thought it was good. Because of the Koolaid and cookies. Some would say, “Can I take some cookies for my brother?” the little ones would say. “Yeah, go ahead,” I told them. And, sometimes, “Can I take some cookies for my mom?” they’d say. “Yeah, go right ahead,” I would tell them. That is how poor they were. And we are doing really good.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, that’s true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And I see, what y’all were saying, bicycles. And, there, they didn’t have tires.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes, they were riding them.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What would they Ones-from-Kenwood say, if they came here? I was thinking.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: [Listening] They are playing music somewhere.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Who is it? ... It’s Choogie.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Is that who? He is playing a guitar.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Choogie?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ryan Mackey’s son, is that him?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I taught him.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When he was little.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The one playing music. Are you a music player?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No, the one playing the music.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I thought you said, “I taught him.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No, at the immersion school, where they learned Cherokee, I taught him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, okay.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I am not a musician!

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I guess I taught him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really, you did.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: A little bit.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I can’t play that. I can play that other one... What do they call, piano?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I don’t know, you press it, I guess.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess that’s it.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I don’t really know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s all it is, but I can play a little bit.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They called it something different. But I don’t remember good. There was an old man that lived, named Charlie Starr. He would just go like this [gestures] and it would play by itself.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He would just do it like this, ain’t it? [gestures]

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: He would say something like ‘bones’.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would call them ‘bones’.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: He would say what he does, but I forget what he said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was a pretty good musician, Charlie Starr.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: He was a very wise musician.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it different now, where you grew up, ‘long time ago? How it was, it’s not like that anymore?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How about, when we were going to school. Do you remember—we were in Ms. Campbell’s room, we wrote those things... Or was I dreaming?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: You must have dreamed it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We all wrote something.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: What was it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We put it in that tree.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Oh yeah. I don’t know if they got it out, I was thinking, found what was written. They did that awhile back. I don’t know what they found. But I remember we wrote something and put it in there. I don’t know. I forgot what we put in there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Me, too. I don’t know what we wrote. Do you remember?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: No, me either.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They probably found those, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They probably found those.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was a long time ago, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: About what year was that?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ahh...

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Maybe the year ‘70 or ‘68. I was born in ‘62 and, if I was six years old, then it was about the year ‘70.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was we about 11 years old?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Was we about that? So it was about the year ‘73.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When did they cut that down, what y’all are saying? That. Y’all put something in there?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I was thinking, before it burned down, I think. I think they did something then.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was it near there? I remember when they dug there, somewhere.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: By the third room—there was a butane bottle. It was close to there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do you think they found those?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I think so. But I don’t know. I didn’t find out what they found.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I was always thinking about it, and forget to say anything to ‘Mona.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: She is thinking, “What did I write?!”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is what I would like to find out. “What did we write?”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was Ms. Campbell, ain’t it? She was scary. I was afraid of her, she was our teacher.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: She would get on to you pretty quick, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What about when we were sewing. We were using material that was dirty to make things. We were taking them apart. Often, we were making those ponchos, ‘had holes in them.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: You had to pull a string, and when you pulled it was straight here. And she would say, “Here,” when we pulled it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t think I did that. We went to school together. I was afraid of her [Ms. Campbell]. And, also those boys were always getting a whipping. Do you remember, for missing what they were spelling? They really got a whipping. Whatever they missed—that was how many.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: When they were spelling. When they missed them [words] they got a whipping.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I didn’t want to miss any.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I didn’t either.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It made a sound when they were getting a whipping.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Every week, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They were getting a hard paddling, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was making a sound.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We were watching them, because it was right there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: She had one she had made out of a board, about this wide [gestures], and she would paddle them with that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: When they made a mistake, they would take them to the head of the school. I had also been there, a few times.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You had been in there a few times.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I can remember, good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you get a whipping, or not?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I used to get a whipping at least once a year.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And also, Ms. Knight she was aggressive, too, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I don’t really think that-One hardly liked us, I think.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No. Us Cherokee, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: When we spoke Cherokee, she would get on to us. And, also, she would say, “Y’all are not going out, unless you be quiet.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh my.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: When we were talking—she didn’t like us talking Cherokee—she would get mad.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You know, when I went to help her for a little while. When I worked there. Ms. Mays told me... Do you remember Maudie Maddox? She told me, “I am going to put you in there.” And so I helped her. We had a good time, Ms. Maddox. Did she teach us?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, in the fourth grade.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We were in the fourth grade.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She was really aggressive when she wanted, but...

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: But she was a friendly woman.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She was funny. Ms. Mays said, “I don’t like it y’all are feeling good.” She said, “I am going to put you in there with Ms. Knight. Y’all are not going to think it is good.” I thought, “Aww...” I was scared. I was thinking, “I’m an adult now.” She put me in there, we were enjoying it. Her son is married to my cousin. Then she got on to us. “Y’all are enjoying this. Now I am going to put you in there with someone mean, ... Ms. Eades.”

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It scared me even more. It was true—she was mean.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: She was, back then.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We have been in there with some pretty mean teachers, ain’t it? But we did good.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We grew up good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I learned. I knew they had hard feelings towards us sometimes, but --

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You couldn’t do anything.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: -- but our dad told us we had to go to school. He said, “To learn. You will have to use it someday.” He said, “Y’all don’t have to speak English, but learn what they are teaching.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They were good teachers, back then.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They were good teachers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me too. I have been hit in the head a few times, because I didn’t speak English. One time I was telling them there was too many of us in there. Cherokee were almost a room full. We didn’t understand nothing, and couldn’t learn anything. There was a few Whites in there, and the teacher was getting on to us, aggressively. We were talking in Cherokee. She was really getting on to us. Back then we would raise the collar up on our shirt. They would be like this [demonstrates]. She was afraid of us, them boys were just doing it. The teacher would walk by and put them down [the collars]. And hit them in the head, and they would go like this [gestures, ducking].

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: How would you say ‘collar’ in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is that? Boy, I forget it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I have heard it before.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me too. I have, too.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: It’s a little bit like ‘neck tie’, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. What is that? ...I really am getting forgetful.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Ayvthlav oyvtlav... I know it. I have heard it, but I forgot.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When I’m going, I get to the house --

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: -- Me too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: -- I will remember. That is what happens.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That is what I am going to be thinking about.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Me too—that is what I am thinking about. Uyatlvdv, is it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Look for it, when you get home.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I am going to look, and see if I have it written down, somewhere.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. When I get back I will ask my wife. I think, yeah, that is what I thought it was.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You know, sometimes I will ask my dad something in Cherokee, when I forget. He will not know.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: He forgets, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: “I forget,” that is why he will not come here.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: He should come here, and speak.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is what I tell him. But he won’t.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: He could start to.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Remembering.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Remembering... If he starts talking to someone.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He says he forgets now.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Those boys talk to him in Cherokee, I mean in English—his grandchildren.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They all don’t know how to speak Cherokee.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, that is why.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My wife speaks pretty good. She remembers the words spoke ‘long time ago. I will ask her sometimes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She will know more.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, and I will ask her what this is written in the Bible. She will quickly tell me. I learn from her.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I just talk to myself.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: It has been like that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t have anyone to talk Cherokee with.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: What else?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What have you done for work?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Not much of anything. I have not worked at very many different things. I started at Cherokee Nation 41 years ago. That was the most part. I worked at Cherokee Nation. I have not moved around a lot. At first I worked where they made the cards, and then at the food distribution. And where they give the children something little to help them. The children, the mother, and the infants—they call it 'W.I.C’.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I worked there for a long time. And for a little while at--what do they call it? It has a name in Cherokee, maintaining health. I think it is called ‘Public Health.’ I worked there for a long time. I was working there. Then I started working over here, at the Cherokee language. [School]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You really worked at Cherokee Nation for a long time.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: It’s been a long time, since I started. I started when I was a child.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: It’s true. Was about 19 years old when I started. And I have been working ever since.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What do you like the most?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Everything.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You like everything?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I enjoyed everything. It was just time for me to do something else.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I didn’t want to go home, but I thought, “I have to do that.” And that is what I thought, when I helped them over here. I could see, “Gaw, we are losing our language.” We are not really losing it, we are just not using it, I was thinking. But the children have to learn. And that is why I told them I would to help them. I really didn’t get hired at first. They just said, “Let’s try it.” For three years we did that. We got very little help. They were not providing money, at first. Not until toward-the-last, the Chief provided that much money.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This-One that is in here?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: This-One that is in here. Every need was fulfilled, to fight for our language to be in use, has been provided. Cherokee Nation has never done that before. It has never provided that much support. And, also, getting help for medical or housing. They have never done that for us, until now. I appreciate it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I thank God for it. Also for the Deputy Chief—he really makes an effort for what is right. He goes to church. For God, I am thankful for that.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: He seems like a nice man.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And the Chief-that-is-in-there, he seems to really want to help the Cherokee people. When he first got in, just as soon as he got in, this Bald-Leader-that-is-here, we stopped at Steeley [Church]. What was we doing at that time? They stopped by there. And the Leader-that-is-there, and his wife, and they said, “We want to have prayer.” “Yeah, we sure can,” they said. You have probably read where Solomon was made king.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yeah. He didn’t want riches.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wisdom was good.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Wisdom.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We prayed for that.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That was good, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He is really doing good now.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That is what he needs to ask for. Not... Not...

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If he asks for wisdom, it will be given to him. He is going to be given something useful.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: On how to do things, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That is what I believe. When Solomon worked, asked back then—That is the same God we have now.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That is the same One-Him, ain’t it? Which is God. He is still the same one, He will be the same all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: All the time, even tomorrow He will be the same.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: He is not going to change.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many siblings did you have? Your sisters and...

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Seven.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Seven.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: All together, there is seven of us children. There is four of us women, and three men.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Three men. All of y’all speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We all spoke Cherokee growing up.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do they just live nearby?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, just close by. The one that lives the furthest away is Yona, she lives towards Chewey. One in Sallisaw. One in Stilwell. And the rest of us just live near where we grew up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When I got here, a little bit ago, I talked to your brother. He said he was going to Albuquerque. Tomorrow, I think he said.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, I think he is going to drive the bus. He is going to take the teachers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He is going to take the teachers?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I don’t know why, I don’t know. The reason they are going is to practice something, or to see how they teach somewhere else. I don’t know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They might learn something there.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: And bring it back.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Bring back to help. That helps.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That way? [Direction]

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: No, this way. The younger ones, the teachers, and the children that teach the little ones.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is where we went, when I was teaching. It was good.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Was it good?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They are not going to fly, are they? They are taking that [bus].

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: No, John is driving.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What are the kids like that live that way? Are they the same as this way?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: The same.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just like we are.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They are just the same, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The kids are doing good, too—out that way, like here?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They are poor.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They are poor, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They speak more in their own language. Or they were speaking... I don’t know how they are now. Five or six [years] before I started here, we went there. Pueblo Indians were there, at the school we went to. The little ones were really talking.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Their own language.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Their own language. But, I don’t know how it is now. They want to speak more English, they are saying. From what I hear. Even here, sometimes, there is Spanish people that work here. I was talking to one, and he was talking about how his family does not want to learn Spanish. “That is the first time I heard anyone that speaks Spanish say that they want to learn English, more.” He said. He said, “You really have to encourage them to speak our language.” That is how much it is different. Just about 10 years ago. That is how much people do not want to speak their own language.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This what an old man was telling me, one time. Do you remember how it’s written somewhere in the Bible they were building to Heaven?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They were building to get to Heaven.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were speaking one language back then, it says. It says, God did not like what they were doing. And, it’s true, it says He gave them different languages. They didn’t understand each other and they just gave up it says. But then He said, “This is what I think now—when it is almost time for the Lord to come back, we will all be speaking one language.” And it is true. We are mostly speaking English. Even if someone from overseas comes and they speak English, we would be talking good. Sometimes I think about that.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Just that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Us Cherokee speak mostly English, sometimes, ain’t it? Even if someone comes from a different tribe comes and speaks English, we will agree good. I am amazed by that. What was your grandpas’ and your grandmas’ names, and also your parents?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: My parents? My mother was Galelo Fayola Duncan.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Duncan.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: ‘Was her name. And her dad’s name was Flynn Duncan. And her mother’s name was Lydia.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Lydia.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Her last name was Eli. And, on this side, my dad’s side, his mother's name was Cora. And his dad was Wash. Cora—Pettit was her last name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is Leo Duncan related to you?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, he is related to me on my mom's side.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you remember, ‘long time ago they would say ‘gadugi’—a long time ago?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I have just heard my dad talking about that. He would say they would say, “Gadugi, all of us together, let’s have an event.” And then, when they would say that, all of us that were neighbors came together, he said. If someone was in need of something, we would try to help them. “If they needed wood, or something to eat, that is what we tried to help him with,” he said. Or a house, like add on a room, or fix the roof—that is what we did. We helped each other, or we ate [together] he said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Or they would be hoeing the garden.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Or they would be clearing fields, he said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What has happened to that?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: If they killed a hog—all the people came.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That I know, we used to do that. Like, if we killed a hog there would be a few of our neighbors that would come early in the morning. They would start as soon as it turned daylight. They would already have a fire built, boiling water. They were always boiling water, but they used a lot of that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And like, for instance, I don’t know if that is what they do toward-where-you-are-from, when someone passed away, they have a wake, a service, where they used to live [at the home]. Do they continue to do that, or just from time to time?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Just from time to time, they still do that. I know when my mother passed away, young people came and they built a fire. They did that for three or four nights. And they were all helping us to clean the house. And they cooked. We did not hardly have to do anything.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is the way it is supposed to be, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That is what they used to do, a long time ago, as I remember. And the women would be cooking and cleaning. And the men would build a fire outside, if it was winter, and be drinking coffee and smoking. They would be doing this with the Prince Albert [tobacco for pipes or roll up cigarettes].

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They were rolling them up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that has stopped. But, then also, y’all looked for things from the woods?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: All the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like, for instance, blueberry, and poke salad.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: In spring it was onion, and poke salad, and kochani. My dad also liked... You can find it right now, if you can find it. It is called uyvhvdi, beans-that-crawl-up. It is ready, if you can find the plant. He used to like them. That is what I mostly remember. And also blackberry, blueberry, and dewberry, and, also, watercress, and fish, and crawdads. And, in the wintertime, Dad would kill rabbits and squirrels. And, as for deer, someone would bring one. Dad did not hardly hunt, he would kill rabbits and squirrels [only].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes, also Grandpa... What would you say? Stayed with us. My dad was imprisoned in the army. He was slim, when he came back. He started drinking around. My mom gave up. She really tried for them to fix it [as a couple]. But alcohol broke it up. My mom was the only one making an effort in raising us, my sister [and me]. My grandpa came to our house, to live with us. Like you said—our second cousin would wear a toe sack or sacks. They put in bread, and go rabbit hunting, and they would bring some [home]. They would all bring some, and then later they would fix them. Later they would be on the table. And it was the same with squirrels. We would really eat them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you cook them?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Oh no, I don’t cook. My mother used to can sometimes [preserve]. Her mother and father her—parents, they had a lot planted. And they would give some to my mother. And that is what Mom canned. She would give some back, or do something for her mother. My mother sewed, and sometimes she would make clothes for this One’s-mother, that-is-sitting-here.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes, your mother has made me some clothes, too. Dresses—she was really good at sewing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh man. She didn’t use flour sacks, did she?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No. But my grandmother used them to make me dresses. I would show off.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: With a flour sack?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We would go to the store, she would say, “Go pick out. We will make you a dress.” So I would go pick one out [a flour sack]. She would make it. I would feel good, and go to school wearing that dress.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: But that was good cloth, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, they would be wearing them good.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: A flour sack.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I was wearing them—no one knew they were flour sacks—and I was showing off.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy, when my mom shopped—the lard was in kinda like tubs, back then. And the potatoes were in hundred-lb bags. And flour, too—it would last a long time, for about a month.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Grandma had one this tall [gestures] it would be full of flour.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We had those metal buckets that used to contain lard. We would sit on them, in the cooking room. When it was time to eat.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Y’all would sit there.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We would sit there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes they would put pillows, or, they would put cloth on them.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We used them for chairs.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That was good, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Our past has been good. It seemed like we barely got by. But, it was not really like that. We were provided things to use, back then.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We learned a lot, growing up like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I know y’all go to church. What about, for instance, have you ever been, or been involved with, at Redbird?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We were not involved in that. Sometimes they would take us over there, and tell us what they do. But we were not members of that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I have never been to a place like that.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I think it is just because we were hungry, that we went.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just to eat.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I think Dad knew. They used to take him a little bit. But Mom did not know anything about it. So, we would only go sometimes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do they eat?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They talk about the past, and the reason they are there. In the preaching they talk about God. Nowadays, they still do that, they still talk about God.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We were discouraged from a place like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Have you heard of Crosslin Smith?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was talking about ‘Red people’ and also ‘Yellow people’, did they believe in that?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: As for me, I couldn’t really say. I don’t really know. I guess they believe that is medicine. If you are talking about that medicine, on how to use it. If you are talking about that, even that, I would not understand it—I don’t know anything about it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I have never been. I, personally, don’t know anything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They made a place-to-go-around at Kenwood, for a little while. But it stopped and faded away. I never did fully understand that either, why they go around.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: There were places everywhere. Nowadays I don’t know if there is four or five places. Or, there still may be seven places.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were there a lot of people that go there, as far as you know? Or, have you heard, still nowadays?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: A long time ago they would stay all day, and then till Sunday. On Saturday night they would dance all night. I think they still do that. When they dance, they dance all night. Then the elders will speak that morning, and then they play ball and eat.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that is true.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess they all cook.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, all the group of clans are given. I forget. It is the same as what is written here—somewhere near to the entrance of the daniyatihiho, supply room, are provided meat to use for that. They are given that to cook, all the time they are there. And, like I was saying, they preach. That is all I know, ‘is just what I have been told. I go visit them, sometimes. Those that I am teaching, they believe half of that, right now. The ones-that-I-am-teaching, now. The ones-I-taught-last-time, did not know anything about that. They didn’t know anything like that. And, the ones-that-are-in-there-now—half of them are members in that. And, also, they participate in that kind of work.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, do they know the reason why they participate?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They say they do.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When I was growing up I never experienced things like that. What about your church, where you go, do all of y’all speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: No. Just our immediate family, that are members there, are the only ones that speak Cherokee. The rest do not speak. But when I was growing up, as a child, that was all we spoke and read. They really did teach like Charlie’s wife, Deyuunegi, Doris. She was the teacher. When I was a child she taught me. She would use the Bible. But it was all in Cherokee. She would teach us all things. Growing up, she taught us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, it was back then you learned Cherokee?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I probably learned a little back then. But I didn’t know how to write, but my reading was OK.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about now, who is y’alls pastor?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We don’t have a pastor. We have a layman that was sent from Salem. His name is Smith.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK. I think he grew up towards where I am from.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: His name is Tim.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Does he preach in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: No. I think his grandfather spoke Cherokee, but he doesn’t speak.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That is true. I think he preaches in all English.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: But we sing in Cherokee. We use both, and also in prayer service.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Both, yeah. That is the way it is where I pastor. But some like the preaching in Cherokee. I use both. Sometimes, when I go somewhere they call me and I mix in Cherokee. “Boy we really appreciate it that we heard it in Cherokee,” they will say.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: It is good to hear someone preaching in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is what, Junior, he uses—Cherokee. And English, he does, because there are some White people in there. That is what he does. And we sing in Cherokee, and then in English. Or he will lead one in English, and finish it in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That is good. What would help the Cherokee language to not fade away and for it to not stop? What could be done for them to feel motivated to learn Cherokee, and not lose it? What do you think about it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Wherever you can use Cherokee language, you should use it. I think the children think that they can only use the Cherokee language here. That is why they do not like speaking outside of here. If the parents could speak outside of here, then they would think it is good that they can speak Cherokee. They will think, “This is how it is supposed to be.” Then they will feel good about speaking. Maybe.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They might learn.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Maybe it might be a little longer.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It really is good that they are teaching them Cherokee here. But they are not teaching them how we talk. It sounds a little different, and it is just straight. How we speak it goes like this [gestures] when we are talking about something. We use our hands, and we use our face, when we Cherokee talk it is like that. And, when we talk about something we really laugh, and think it is funny. If you tell them in English, the reason we are laughing --

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: -- It doesn’t make sense. It is not that funny.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It don’t, does it? We, I, was teaching. They would bring their parents, and they would say, “We don’t know what our children are saying, because we don’t speak Cherokee.” There was a lot of them that were like that. “We don’t understand. We, my husband, can’t speak to them. We don’t know what they are saying,” they would say.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That is what I do now, when I get done on Thursday evenings. Over there. I teach the parents of the children, for one hour.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really? You really are doing good.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: It seems like they are using it more.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is there a lot that come?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, all the parents come.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They have to be here, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes, they are made to come. But they seem to feel good about it. They don’t seem to be troubled. It is really good. They feel good about it. They are happy when they come.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s good that it’s like that.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They try to write, and say it. And they ask, “What can I say to them?” They want to know what to say to them. And, sometimes, they bring their children. So, I start with talking to them [the children]. So when they see it, [the parents], they seem to feel good about the little children learning. They seem like they have to learn. According to the look on their face, I have hope that they want to learn.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Praise the Lord. ‘Is very joyful that is what the parents are doing. Like you said, if some parents realize what the children are doing here, and what you are doing is good. It turns out good. They are realizing it now.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: That it is important. And, that they are learning. When they see me talking to them, they seem to be amazed by it. “My child can really understand, they can really speak.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I could be doing that.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I have hope that is what they are thinking.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really. Some White people say that Cherokee is the most beautiful language. And, also, the singing in Cherokee makes a beautiful sound, they say. And it’s true, that is what I think, too. When I think about it real good. I don’t know if you have... I don’t know if you have ever been, a long time ago, over there, or have y’all hardly ever been where they call the ‘assembly ground’?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There would be a full house. They would be singing in all Cherokee. It was a beautiful sound.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: We have never been there. We were not members there, at the church we were a part of.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would make a beautiful sound.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They would camp, long time ago, at Bible school.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yes, Bible school.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Bible school—we would go there all the time. It would be hot. We used to spend the night. Back then, they did not have AC. We raised the windows up. We used to make our clothes and bed wet, from the heat.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I remember, every now and then, about 300 or 400 would come for a whole week. ‘Like you said, they would spend the night.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Hurry up, I’m just saying that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What else do you want to talk about?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Is that as far as you asking questions?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There is more. But talk about what you are thinking of. What is going to happen to the Cherokee language, like you were saying earlier.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Or, as the children are growing up. Or, what is it going to be like when they grow up?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: These children that are learning right now, what is it going to be like? Are they going to want and continue to learn? I wonder about that. The same with these adults that I am teaching, now. Some are getting hired here, and they continue to learn. If it is like that, they are going to learn. There is several of them that have finished here. We talk good. I speak to them in Cherokee, and, when they answer me back they speak in Cherokee. They don’t want to use any English. If that is the way they feel, there will still be Cherokee speakers when we are gone.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It not be that good.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They will not say what we can say. And, also, they have to experience that, to grow. Before they can know about what we are talking about. And, if they have not experienced that [while] being raised, they are not really going to know. That is why it is different in the way they speak. I think. I think they will still be talking.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It will be joyful, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: Yes. But I do not know if they will be saying what we are saying.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: It could be better.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It could be talking better.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They might be talking better. I do know that if you teach them something, and sometimes we forget, they will know. If I teach them something, and tell them to write it down, and remember what I said. And, then later, if I forget. They already know. And say, “That is what you said.” I appreciate that they do that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They pay attention.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: They remember easy—that is the way it is. They remember easy. My hope is they are going to use it. And those little children will know what they are saying. Even now those little children know what they are saying. They know what is going on. One is Joe Bird’s grandchild. I am always talking to that-One in Cherokee. They have been in there since they were a little baby. And that is... they speak when we talk. They don’t speak fully, but that is the way a child is. They are not going to speak fully. But they are going to understand. For the linguistics, if you know the root, you will know what you are saying, they say. And, also, and you will know when to use it. What to put in front, and what to put behind it. The sound—you will know the front sound. You will know. Some are learning a lot of that, they are learning good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That is good, it makes me happy that I heard that.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I think some speakers don’t know... I don’t think they know how hard the work is. When I first started, I was thinking, “How am I going to teach? What am I going to be saying?” So, I started watching that is... What you say. That is, what we were saying. I have never thought about what we were saying [before that]. We were just saying it. We were speaking. The reason was—that is what we knew.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is what we knew, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: It was what we knew. Now, they have to think about it. But, there is going to come a time, the little ones will know, it will be deep within them. All the Cherokee still have that within them. That is where we come from, it is within us to learn. That is what I tell the adults—that is within them. “The reason is, somewhere your grandmother or your grandfather, or both, were speakers,” I was telling them. You will know, if that is the way you were raised, I was telling them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that is what I think, too, God has given us our Cherokee language. And, if God gives you something and you don’t use it, He might take it back. And, if we don’t use the Cherokee language, we are going to lose it. Sometimes that is what I think.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: It makes you wonder, sometimes, about that, it has happened.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, Cora, I appreciate it.

segments.speaker: cora-flute
segments.translation: I appreciate it, too.
